turns.question: What's the latest stable version of Node.js?
turns.answer:
**Node.js 26.13.0 "Lithium"** is the latest stable release as of 10 Nov 2026 — it's also the current LTS line [16][17][18].

- Released 28 Oct 2026, and it's the release that moved Node 26 into Active LTS; the only change from 26.12.1 is the LTS metadata, so nothing new feature-wise [17][18]. Support runs to end of April 2029 [17].
- 26 is the last line under the old twice-yearly model; from Node 27 (alpha started 28 Oct 2026, first release April 2027) there's one major per year, every one becoming LTS [1][5][15].
- Node 24 and 22 are now in Maintenance [7].

One caveat: the project has announced security releases for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines "on or shortly after" Wednesday 11 November 2026, addressing a HIGH-severity issue, so a 26.13.1-class patch should appear tomorrow [3][6]. I couldn't confirm a build newer than 26.13.0 published before today.

turns.question: Compare Neon and Supabase free tiers.
turns.answer:
**Neon is far more generous on free database capacity and project count; Supabase gives you a fuller application stack (auth, storage, realtime, functions, 50k MAU) on a much smaller database.**

| | Neon Free | Supabase Free |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $0 | $0 |
| Projects | 100 [11] | 2 active (more allowed if paused) [1] |
| Postgres storage | 1 GB per project, 20 GB total across all projects [11] | 500 MB per project [1] |
| Compute | 100 CU-hours per project/month, autoscaling 0.25–2 CU (about 8 GB RAM) [11] | Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM [1] |
| Inactivity | Scales to zero after 5 min idle, first query takes a few hundred ms [11][8] | Project paused after 1 week idle; serves nothing until restored [1][8] |
| Egress | 5 GB per project/month [11] | 5 GB + 5 GB cached (10 GB total) [1][14] |
| Branches | 10 per project (copy-on-write) [11] | Not applicable |
| Auth | Managed Better Auth up to 60,000 MAU [12] | 50,000 MAU [1] |
| Functions | 1M invocations per project/month [12] | 500K invocations [4] |
| File storage | 5 GB object storage per project [6] | 1 GB [1] |
| Backups/snapshots | 1 manual snapshot; no scheduled backups [5] | No backups [8] |

Practical read: Neon suits database-heavy work where you want many separate databases or branches and fast, cheap numbers — and its per-project allowances (100 CU-hours, 5 GB egress) beat Supabase's account-wide ones by a wide margin. Supabase suits a single app that needs auth, file storage, realtime and edge functions, but the 500 MB database and week-long pause make it a demo tier rather than something to run a live site on.

Not verified: exact Supabase free quotas for realtime messages and peak connections (the older changelog gives 2M messages and 200 connections [13], but I didn't find a current page confirming those), and current Neon free limits on branch count beyond 10 per project.

turns.question: Our API serves 1.2 million requests a day. The busiest hour carries 15% of the daily traffic, and each request uses 80 ms of CPU on one core. Our autoscaler targets 60% CPU. How many cores do we need at peak? And is a 60% target sensible if p99 latency has to stay under 200 ms?
turns.answer:
**7 cores** (round up from 6.67) — and 60% is defensible on average queueing maths but too tight to promise a 200 ms p99 without checking the tail.

**The arithmetic**
- Peak hour: 15% of 1.2M = 180,000 requests → 50 req/s
- CPU work: 50 × 0.08 s = **4 cores' worth**, sustained
- At a 60% target: 4 / 0.6 = 6.67 → **7 cores** (8 if you want N+1 so a single instance/zone loss still leaves you under target: 4/7 = 57%)

**On the 60% target and p99**
Modelling each core as a server with 4 erlangs offered to 7 servers (57% utilisation), about 13% of requests queue at all, mean wait is ~4 ms and the 99th-percentile wait is roughly 70 ms — so total p99 ≈ 150 ms, inside a 200 ms budget but with only ~50 ms of margin. That margin is fragile:

- The model assumes short, well-behaved service times. If the 80 ms is the *mean* and p99 CPU per request is 2× that, the SLO is already at risk at 57%.
- Real tails (GC, cold caches, retries, a noisy neighbour on the same host, coordinated omission in your load test) all land in p99, not the mean.
- At 60% you have 1.67× headroom; queueing delay grows sharply above ~70–80%, so a 30-second traffic spike eats the margin fast.

Practically: target **50% at peak** (8 cores, one core of failure tolerance) and autoscale on concurrency or RPS against a latency SLO rather than CPU alone — with 80 ms requests, CPU target is a coarse proxy.

**One thing to verify:** 15% of daily traffic in an hour is 50 req/s *averaged over that hour*. If your busiest minute runs 2× that (common), you need 8 CPU-seconds → **14 cores at a 60% target**. Pull minute-level data before sizing.

turns.question: We're 4 engineers running a Django monolith on one EC2 instance, with Postgres on the same machine. Traffic doubled this quarter, and every deploy causes about 30 seconds of downtime. What should we change first, and what should we deliberately not do yet?
turns.answer:
Move the app onto two instances behind a load balancer, with the database on managed Postgres — that fixes the deploy downtime and the single point of failure in one move. Everything else can wait.

**Do first, roughly in this order**

1. **Measure for a day before changing anything.** Per-request p95, DB CPU and connection count, slow query log, and whether the box is CPU-, memory- or IO-bound. Doubled traffic on one box is usually 2–3 bad queries plus a missing index, not a capacity problem.
2. **Two app instances behind a load balancer, with rolling deploys and health checks.** This is the cheapest fix for 30 seconds of downtime and it also gives you N+1 redundancy. Watch for the landmines that only appear with two servers: sessions in local memory, uploads to local disk, `lru_cache`, cron running inside the web process, in-process rate limits.
3. **Make migrations expand/contract** so you can deploy code and schema independently: add nullable columns, backfill, switch reads, drop later. Never a destructive migration in the same release as the code change.
4. **Managed Postgres (RDS/Cloud SQL), with PITR and automated backups.** Prerequisite for step 2 anyway, and the one thing that is genuinely painful to retrofit. Turn on PgBouncer/connection pooling at the same time — Django's per-worker connections will exhaust the DB before CPU does.
5. **Then the boring multipliers:** background jobs out of the request cycle (Celery/RQ), static and media to S3 + CDN, Redis for cache and sessions.

**Deliberately not yet**

- **Microservices or splitting the monolith.** Four engineers, one deploy unit — this adds coordination cost and fixes no latency.
- **Kubernetes.** An ASG or ECS with two tasks is enough; K8s is a second job.
- **Sharding, read replicas for read traffic, multi-region.** A standby replica for failover is fine; routing reads is a measured decision, not a precaution.
- **Self-managed Postgres HA** (Patroni, streaming replication you operate). You don't have the headcount to run it well.
- **A rewrite or a language change.** Traffic doubled; the code didn't get worse.

The one legitimate shortcut: if step 1 shows you're simply CPU-bound and clean, resize the instance this week as a stopgap — just don't let it be the strategy for the third doubling.

turns.question: Which of Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages has the most generous free tier for a static site that uses about 200 GB of bandwidth a month, and what happens with each one if I go past its free limit?
turns.answer:
**Cloudflare Pages, by a wide margin**: its free tier has no bandwidth cap at all, so 200 GB/month costs nothing. Vercel (100 GB) and Netlify (effectively ~15 GB, since its free plan is now credit-based) would both fail well before 200 GB.

| | Free bandwidth | What 200 GB/month costs | What happens if you exceed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cloudflare Pages** | Unlimited, on every plan ("unlimited sites, seats, requests, and bandwidth") [10][13] | $0 | Nothing to exceed on bandwidth. The free tier's real caps are elsewhere — 500 builds/month, then builds are blocked until next month [4][8] |
| **Vercel (Hobby)** | 100 GB "Fast Data Transfer" per month [3][7][9] | Not possible on Hobby — you'd have to move to Pro at $20/seat/month (includes $20 usage) [5][9] | You can't buy extra on Hobby: "in most cases" the feature stays off and you wait 30 days for the limit to reset, and Vercel may take the site offline until then [3][9][14]. Also personal, non-commercial use only [9] |
| **Netlify (Free)** | Not a GB allowance any more: 300 credits/month at 20 credits per GB of bandwidth [15][19] | ~4,000 credits needed for 200 GB → roughly Pro (3,000 credits, $20/mo) plus credit packs ($10 per 1,500 credits) [17][19] | Hard limit: projects **pause** until the next billing cycle (every site on the account), showing a "Site not available" page; they can't incur overage charges unless you upgrade or enable auto-recharge [12][20] |

Two caveats worth knowing:

- **Netlify's older accounts** created before 4 Sep 2025 can stay on legacy plans with 100 GB bandwidth, then $55 per extra 100 GB on Starter, or a hard limit on Free [11]. New signups get the credits model, where 200 GB of bandwidth alone is over 13× the free allowance [15][21].
- Check whether your traffic is cached: on Vercel only "Fast Data Transfer" (cache-served) is free up to 100 GB, while Fast Origin Transfer, which is traffic served uncached from origin, has its own 10 GB allowance [3][7]. A static site served from the CDN mostly uses the former, but 200 GB would still roughly double the free cap.

So unless you specifically need Vercel's framework features or Netlify's forms/functions, Cloudflare Pages is the only one of the three where 200 GB/month is comfortably free.

turns.question: Compare Neon and Supabase free tiers.
turns.answer:
Both cost $0, but they differ in shape: Neon gives you more Postgres per project and lots of projects, while Supabase bundles auth, storage, Edge Functions and realtime — with a much smaller database and inactivity pausing.

| | Neon (Free) | Supabase (Free) |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $0 | $0 |
| Projects | 100 [5][6] | 2 active, unlimited paused [1][9] |
| Storage | 1 GB per project, 20 GB across account [5][6] | 500 MB database [1][12] |
| Compute | 100 CU-hours per project/month, autoscaling up to 2 CU (~8 GB RAM) [5][10] | Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM [12] |
| Idle behaviour | Compute scales to zero after 5 min, can't disable [5][11] | Project paused after 1 week of inactivity [1][12] |
| Branching | 10 branches per project [5][6] | Not on free plan |
| Network transfer | 5 GB per project/month [5][6] | 5 GB egress + 5 GB cached egress [12] |
| Extras | Postgres only; Better Auth up to 60k MAU, 6h instant restore [5][6] | Auth (50k MAU), 1 GB file storage, 500k Edge Function invocations, realtime, unlimited API requests [1][3][4][12] |

Practical read: Neon is the better free Postgres if you want several separate databases (dev/staging/prod, per-customer projects) or branching for preview environments — 100 CU-hours per project is roughly a 0.25 CU compute running 400 hours/month [10]. Supabase is better if you want the whole backend in one place, but 500 MB of database fills quickly and free projects go to sleep after a week idle.

One caveat: Neon's older docs still list the old free limits (10 projects, 0.5 GB storage, 191.9 compute hours) [7][8]. The current FAQ and docs, updated 2026, give the 100-project/1 GB figures above, so I've used those.

turns.question: Is it still free if I go over the limits?
turns.answer:
Yes — on both, going over the free limits never produces a bill. Both hard-stop instead, but they stop in different places.

**Neon** explicitly "does not bill overages on the Free plan" [5][6]. What happens depends on the limit:

- **CU-hours or 5 GB network transfer used up:** that project's compute is suspended — existing connections drop, new ones can't open — until the next monthly billing period or until you upgrade [5][6]. Your data stays in storage and counts against the 1 GB cap [6].
- **Over 1 GB storage in a project:** inserts, updates and deletes that would grow storage fail until you free space or upgrade [5][17]. Reads keep working.
- **Over 20 GB total across all projects:** storage-growing operations fail account-wide [6].
- **Over 100 projects:** new project creation fails until you delete one [5].

Compute and network transfer reset monthly; storage, branch and project counts don't [5].

**Supabase** also charges nothing on Free — "you will not be charged while using the Free Plan" [19]. Instead:

- Exceeding quotas (database size, egress and so on) gets your project **restricted**: it returns HTTP 402 with a code like `exceed_egress_quota` or `exceed_db_size_quota` [15]. You keep dashboard access to your data [15].
- Restrictions come under the Fair Use Policy, so persistently exceeding limits is what triggers them [15][19].
- Separately, free projects pause after a week of inactivity and can't serve requests until you unpause them [1][15].

The practical difference: Neon suspends compute or blocks writes per limit and lifts it automatically at the next billing period; Supabase restricts the whole project under its fair-use rules, and enforcement is less mechanical about when it resets. Neither asks for a card on Free, so there's nothing to charge anyway.

turns.question: Remind me what we went over on the 3rd, and does it still hold?
turns.answer:
On the 3rd we compared entry paid managed Postgres plans — Neon Launch, Supabase Pro, Render Basic-256mb and AWS RDS db.t4g.micro — and I said Render was the cheapest entry point. Checking again today, the Supabase and AWS figures still hold, but the Render number was wrong and the Neon figure needs correcting.

| Item | Then (3 Nov 2026) | Now (10 Nov 2026) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neon | Launch plan "about $19/month" | No monthly minimum or per-project fee at all; pay per CU-hour, with compute at $0.106/CU-hour and "typical spend about $15/month" on Launch for a small database [15][16][18] | Changed / corrected |
| Supabase | Pro $25/month per project, 8 GB DB storage | Pro from $25/month, includes one Micro instance and 8 GB disk [1][3][4][13] | Unchanged |
| Render | Basic-256mb Postgres "about $6/month" | Current 256 MB compute plan is $20/month [11]; the only 256 MB tier near $6 is the legacy Starter at $7/month, which can't be used for new databases [7][8] | Changed / was wrong |
| AWS RDS | db.t4g.micro single-AZ ~$12/month | $0.016/hour in US East (N. Virginia), about $11.68/month before storage [20][22][23] | Unchanged |

Two things follow. First, the "$19 monthly Launch plan" framing was never quite right — Neon's paid plans are usage-based with no base fee, and the docs put a typical small Launch database closer to $15/month [15]. Second, Render is not the cheapest entry point: on current list prices a single-AZ db.t4g.micro at about $11.68/month plus storage beats its $20/month 256 MB Postgres plan, and I can't find any $6 Postgres tier on Render's page [11][20]. I couldn't confirm when Render's 256 MB plan moved to $20, only that the $7 legacy tier is closed to new databases [7][8].

So the shortlist ordering flips: AWS RDS cheapest, then Neon, then Supabase, with Render now the priciest of the four.
